summary: Defines the standard algorithm TCP senders are required to use to compute and manage their retransmission timer. It was later replaced by RFC 6298.

plainLanguage.summary: When TCP sends data, it waits for a reply before sending it again. This RFC fixes how long that wait should be, so a sender is neither too hasty nor too slow to retransmit. The sender tracks how long a round trip usually takes and how much that varies, and waits a little longer than the usual time.

subtitle: The algorithm a TCP sender uses to decide how long to wait before retransmitting unacknowledged data.

tldr.problem: A TCP sender that retransmits too early floods the path, and one that retransmits too late wastes time and slows the connection down.
tldr.mechanism: The sender keeps a smoothed average round-trip time and a measure of how much that average varies, and sets the timeout to the average plus four times the variation, never below one second.
tldr.outcome: The algorithm became a MUST for TCP implementations. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 6298.

facts.label: Heartbeat timer lower bound
facts.value: 2.5 seconds, or 2.5 + G seconds with a heartbeat timer

today: RFC 2988 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6298, so read that document for the current rules.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) uses a retransmission timer to ensure data delivery in the absence of any feedback from the remote data receiver. The duration of this timer is called the RTO, the retransmission timeout. RFC 1122 specifies that the RTO should be calculated as outlined in the 1988 paper by Van Jacobson, and this document codifies that algorithm. It expands on the discussion in section 4.2.3.1 of RFC 1122 and upgrades the requirement of supporting the algorithm from a SHOULD to a MUST.

The RFC also notes that in some situations it may be beneficial for a TCP sender to be more conservative than the algorithms here allow, but a TCP MUST NOT be more aggressive than the algorithms allow.
sections.plainLanguage: When TCP sends data, it waits for a reply before sending it again. This RFC fixes how long that wait should be, so that a sender is neither too hasty nor too slow to retransmit.

sections.title: The Basic Algorithm
sections.content:
To compute the current RTO, a TCP sender maintains two state variables, SRTT, the smoothed round-trip time, and RTTVAR, the round-trip time variation, and assumes a clock granularity of G seconds.

  • Until a round-trip time measurement has been made for a segment sent between the sender and receiver, the sender SHOULD set RTO to 3 seconds, though the backing off on repeated retransmission still applies. A lower bound of 2.5 seconds is also acceptable for a heartbeat timer, provided the timer never expires faster than 2.5 seconds. A heartbeat timer with a granularity of G SHOULD not set the timer below 2.5 + G seconds.
  • When the first RTT measurement R is made, the host MUST set SRTT to R, RTTVAR to R/2, and RTO to SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR), where K = 4.
  • When a subsequent measurement R' is made, the host MUST set RTTVAR to (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'|, then SRTT to (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R', using the value of SRTT from before it was updated. The update SHOULD use alpha = 1/8 and beta = 1/4. After the computation, the host MUST update RTO to SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR).
  • Whenever RTO is computed, if it is less than 1 second then the RTO SHOULD be rounded up to 1 second.
  • A maximum value MAY be placed on RTO provided it is at least 60 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a running average of how long a round trip takes, and a measure of how much that average varies. The timeout is that average plus four times the variation, and never less than one second.

sections.title: Taking RTT Samples
sections.content:
TCP MUST use Karn's algorithm for taking RTT samples. That is, RTT samples MUST NOT be made using segments that were retransmitted, because for those it is ambiguous whether the reply was for the first instance of the packet or a later one. The only case when TCP can safely take RTT samples from retransmitted segments is when the TCP timestamp option is employed, since the timestamp option removes the ambiguity about which instance of the data segment triggered the acknowledgment.

Traditionally, TCP implementations have taken one RTT measurement at a time, typically once per RTT. When the timestamp option is used, each ACK can be used as an RTT sample, and RFC 1323 suggests that connections utilizing large congestion windows should take many RTT samples per window of data to avoid aliasing effects in the estimated RTT. A TCP implementation MUST take at least one RTT measurement per RTT, unless that is not possible under Karn's algorithm.

For fairly modest congestion window sizes, research suggests that timing each segment does not lead to a better RTT estimator. Also, when multiple samples are taken per RTT, the alpha and beta defined in section 2 may keep an inadequate RTT history.
sections.plainLanguage: A measurement must come from a segment that was not retransmitted, because otherwise the reply could belong to either copy. The timestamp option makes that safe, because it says which copy was acknowledged.

sections.title: Clock Granularity
sections.content:
There is no requirement for the clock granularity G used for computing RTT measurements and the state variables. However, if the K*RTTVAR term in the RTO calculation equals zero, the variance term MUST be rounded to G seconds, so the calculation becomes RTO <- SRTT + max (G, K*RTTVAR).

Experience has shown that finer clock granularities, of 100 msec or less, perform somewhat better than more coarse granularities. The 1988 paper by Van Jacobson outlines several tricks that can be used to obtain better precision from coarse granularity timers, and these changes are widely implemented in current TCP implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The clock a sender uses to time the round trip limits how precise the timeout can be. The RFC sets no rule for it, but says a clock of a tenth of a second or finer works better than a coarse one.

sections.title: Managing the RTO Timer
sections.content:
An implementation MUST manage the retransmission timer so that a segment is never retransmitted too early, that is, less than one RTO after the previous transmission of that segment. The recommended algorithm is as follows.

  • Every time a packet containing data is sent, including a retransmission, if the timer is not running, start it running so that it will expire after RTO seconds.
  • When all outstanding data has been acknowledged, turn off the retransmission timer.
  • When an ACK is received that acknowledges new data, restart the retransmission timer so that it will expire after RTO seconds.
  • When the timer expires, retransmit the earliest segment that has not been acknowledged by the TCP receiver.
  • The host MUST set RTO to RTO * 2, which is the backing off of the timer. The maximum value from rule 2.5 may provide an upper bound for the doubling.
  • Start the retransmission timer so that it expires after RTO seconds, for the value of RTO after the doubling.

After retransmitting, once a new RTT measurement is obtained, the computations of section 2 are performed again, including the computation of RTO, which may result in collapsing RTO back down after it has been subject to exponential backoff. A TCP implementation MAY clear SRTT and RTTVAR after backing off the timer multiple times, since the current values are likely to be bogus in that situation, and once cleared they should be initialized with the next RTT sample using rule 2.2 rather than rule 2.3.
sections.plainLanguage: The timer runs while data is outstanding. Each new acknowledgement restarts it. When it expires the oldest unacknowledged segment is sent again, and the waiting time is doubled so the sender does not flood the path.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document requires a TCP to wait for a given interval before retransmitting an unacknowledged segment. An attacker could cause a TCP sender to compute a large value of RTO by adding delay to a timed packet's latency, or to its acknowledgment. However, the ability to add delay to a packet's latency often coincides with the ability to cause the packet to be lost, so it is difficult to see what an attacker would gain from such an attack beyond what simply discarding some of the connection's packets would cause.

The Internet relies to a considerable degree on correct implementation of the RTO algorithm, and on the algorithms of RFC 2581, in order to preserve network stability and avoid congestion collapse. An attacker could cause TCP endpoints to respond more aggressively in the face of congestion by forging acknowledgments for segments before the receiver has actually received the data, thus lowering RTO to an unsafe value. Doing so requires spoofing the acknowledgments correctly, which is difficult unless the attacker can monitor traffic along the path between the sender and the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the path can delay a packet or forge an acknowledgement to make the sender retransmit more or less often than it should. Both attacks are hard to do without being able to see the connection's traffic.

data.title: Computing the RTO
data.code:
first measurement R:
    SRTT  <- R
    RTTVAR <- R/2
    RTO   <- SRTT + max (G, K*RTTVAR)

later measurement R':
    RTTVAR <- (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'|
    SRTT   <- (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R'
    RTO    <- SRTT + max (G, K*RTTVAR)

items.title: Start the timer
items.text: Every time a packet containing data is sent, including a retransmission, start the timer if it is not running so that it expires after RTO seconds.

items.title: Stop the timer
items.text: When all outstanding data has been acknowledged, turn off the retransmission timer.

items.title: Restart on new data
items.text: When an ACK arrives that acknowledges new data, restart the timer so that it expires after RTO seconds.

items.title: Retransmit
items.text: When the timer expires, retransmit the earliest segment the receiver has not acknowledged.

items.title: Back off
items.text: The host MUST set RTO to RTO * 2, and the maximum value may provide an upper bound for that doubling.

items.title: Restart after backoff
items.text: Start the timer so that it expires after RTO seconds, for the value of RTO after the doubling.
